Cygnus olor initiates reproduction when females produce clutches ranging from 4 to 10 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 4 to 10 eggs per nest] and typically complete one nesting cycle each year [F_R_i = one nesting cycle each year], which represents the maximum laying rate under optimal conditions at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Eggs deposited in the large cup nests require a sustained incubation period of approximately 36 days [ab = approximately 36 days] when maintained at the average nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that facilitates proper embryonic development within the calcareous shell. Hatchlings emerge covered in downy plumage and exhibit a wet weight at birth averaging 157 grams [Wwb = 157 grams], reflecting the substantial maternal investment in yolk reserves and albumen-buffered egg contents. This neonatal mass is relatively high among Anatidae, indicative of the semi-precocial developmental mode in which chicks are capable of swimming and self-feeding soon after hatching.

Fledging in this species occurs approximately 135 days after hatching [tx = approximately 135 days after hatching] at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which corresponds to the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods. The flight feather maturation process that enables nest departure is relatively protracted compared to smaller waterfowl, a consequence of the large body size and the extended period required for wing loading to reach a sustainable threshold. During this nestling phase, the developing chick undergoes a period of rapid mass gain, ultimately attaining the substantial body dimensions characteristic of one of the heaviest volant birds. The age at fledging can vary between 120 and 150 days depending on local food availability and parental provisioning rates, but the central tendency documented across multiple populations converges on the 135-day figure in monitored colonies across northern Europe.

The time since birth at puberty for male mute swans has been estimated at 405 days [tp = 405 days] at a standard metabolic body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This milestone, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and testosterone surge, is reached considerably later than fledging, as young birds require additional months to complete somatic growth and develop the complete adult plumage. Subadult individuals are often identifiable by their greyish-brown feathers that persist through the first winter before the white breeding plumage emerges. The post-fledging dispersal period involves juveniles moving to communal feeding grounds where they form loose aggregations, particularly in estuarine habitats, before seeking vacant territories. Puberty represents a critical life-history transition that must be attained before any reproductive activity can commence.

First successful breeding events in Cygnus olor are recorded at 1095 days since birth [tR = 1095 days since birth] at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], under the thermal conditions typical of the species. This substantial delay between reaching puberty and initiating a first brood reflects the intense competition for high-quality nesting territories and the time required to form stable pair bonds, which in this species are often maintained for life. Newly formed pairs engage in elaborate courtship displays and may construct multiple trial nests before selecting a final site. The deferred onset of reproduction is a common pattern among long-lived waterfowl, allowing individuals to accumulate the necessary experience and fat reserves to successfully incubate a clutch and rear the altricial nestlings. This extended prereproductive period contributes to the comparatively slow life-history strategy observed in the species.

Maximum recorded longevity for Cygnus olor in the wild reaches approximately 14600 days [am = approximately 14600 days] at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a duration that equates to roughly 40 years for the oldest documented individuals. This remarkable lifespan places the mute swan among the most long-lived of all waterfowl, exceeded only by certain large seabirds and some captive Anatidae specimens. Females attain an ultimate wet weight reaching up to 10.6 kilograms [Wwi = up to 10.6 kilograms], while males are substantially heavier, achieving an adult body mass of up to 14.3 kilograms [Wwi = up to 14.3 kilograms]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males exceeding females by over 35% in body mass, is among the most extreme documented in any swan species and is thought to be associated with male-male competition for territories. Senescence eventually leads to a gradual decline in reproductive output and physiological performance before natural mortality occurs.
